nodes.label: Wild canes
nodes.full: S. robustum on New Guinea and the islands east of the Wallace line is the wild ancestor of the sweet cane; S. spontaneum ranges across Asia and later supplies the hybrid partner.

nodes.label: Kuk Swamp
nodes.full: Wetland cultivation in the New Guinea Highlands, dated from about 10,000 years ago (Golson and Hughes) or about 7,000 (Denham): the agricultural landscape in which cane was domesticated. Cane itself is not attested at Kuk in the chapter read.

nodes.label: Domestication
nodes.full: Sugarcane is domesticated from wild robustum cane in New Guinea and nearby islands by selecting plants with sugar-rich pith, about 8,000 years ago on the genomic dating.
nodes.src: Garsmeur et al. (2025) via CIRAD; Denham (2025)

nodes.label: Brandes model
nodes.full: The older account: three diffusions from New Guinea, the first c.8000 BC and the second, perhaps two thousand years later, to the Philippines and India.

nodes.label: Island voyagers
nodes.full: Migrating peoples carry cane through Melanesia and Polynesia between about 3,500 and 500 years ago, where it hybridises with a previously unknown ancestor and with Miscanthus.

nodes.label: Austronesian word
nodes.full: Sugarcane has a reconstructed Proto-Austronesian name, continued in Proto-Malayo-Polynesian and Proto-Oceanic: a named crop of the speakers who spread from Taiwan.
nodes.src: Blust via Wikipedia ‘Sugarcane’; Ross, Pawley & Osmond

nodes.label: Bee limit
nodes.full: No Neolithic beeswax is found north of the 57th parallel, the authors’ reading of the honeybee’s northern limit.

nodes.label: Beeswax pots
nodes.full: Beeswax residues in Neolithic cooking pots, the oldest from seventh-millennium BC Turkey, show early farmers exploiting honeybee products.
nodes.src: Roffet-Salque et al. (2015) via press summaries

nodes.label: Abu Ghurab bees
nodes.full: A relief in Niuserre’s sun temple shows hive beekeeping — smoke, combs, strained honey sealed in jars.

edges: Sugarcane was domesticated from the wild cane S. robustum, which grows on New Guinea and the islands east of the Wallace line.
Domestication happened inside the New Guinea agricultural landscape that Kuk documents, though the Kuk chapter does not itself mention cane.
Brandes’s model sends the first diffusions out of the New Guinea centre of domestication, a reading the genomic work revises.
The press release places the island centre of diversification where S. officinarum was introduced during Melanesian migrations.
The reconstructed Austronesian words show cane as a named crop of the island-voyaging peoples who carried it.
The authors read the absence of beeswax north of 57°N as the honeybee’s ecological limit, which bounds where the wax can appear in the pots.
Neolithic exploitation of honeybee products precedes the managed hive shown at Abu Ghurab by some four thousand years.
